title: Reaction network graph: how is the chemistry connected?
summary: Species as nodes sized by flux and reactions as arrows with width equal to flux, laid out from reactants on the left to products on the right. It shows the dominant pathway and the branches around it.

media.alt: Node-link diagram of hydrogen-oxygen chemistry with circles for species sized by flux and arrows with widths for reaction flux, ending at water.
media.caption: Reference render with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery).

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: How is the chemistry connected?
read_the_figure.axes: No numeric axes. Position is layout only. Node area encodes net flux through the species, arrow width encodes reaction flux, colour encodes role: amber reactants, teal intermediates, rose product.
look_at: Which arrow is the widest, and where does it end?
Which nodes are largest? They carry the most throughput.
Are there thin side branches (HO2, H2O2) that carry little flux?
Does an arrow pass behind a node it does not touch?
read_the_figure.proves: It shows the topology and the dominant route from fuel to product at one operating condition: which species feed which, where the flux concentrates.
if_wrong: Arrows without a stated scale: width has no meaning.
Layout that suggests a reaction order or a time axis: position is arbitrary unless said otherwise.
Crossing or overlapping arrows: a connection looks real that is not.

terms.meaning: A species. Its area here is proportional to the net flux through it.
A reaction path from a reactant species to a product species, drawn as an arrow.
Rate of conversion along a path, in mol per volume per time, often normalised to the fuel consumption.
A chain of edges from fuel to products; the dominant pathway has the largest flux along the chain.
Integer coefficients that tell how many moles of each species a reaction makes or consumes.

remember: Node area ~ flux through it, edge width ~ reaction flux, as the caption says.
Arrow direction is forward flux; a net reverse is drawn the other way or omitted.
The layout is not data: distance means nothing.
State the conditions (T, p, time or progress) of the flux snapshot.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Circles encode species, area encodes net flux, and the fill colour encodes role (reactant, intermediate, product). Arrows encode reaction paths with line width equal to the flux and a small arrowhead for direction. Text inside the node names the species. The caption is the legend.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: A mechanism is a graph before it is a table of numbers: species are connected by reactions. A node-link diagram shows connectivity at a glance and a size or width channel puts the quantity next to the connections. The question 'how is the chemistry connected' has the answer 'through OH, mostly', which the eye finds immediately in the large hub in the centre.

understand.title: Read this reference render
understand.text: Q1: What is the dominant pathway? The widest arrow runs from OH to H2O (width near 1.0 on the figure's scale), and the next widest feed OH from H and from O: H2 to H to OH to H2O is the main chain. Q2: Which species carry the least flux? H2O2 and HO2, the smallest teal circles, with thin arrows (0.08 to 0.3). Q3: Does H2 feed OH directly? There is an arrow from H2 to OH, but it is drawn through the H node; the figure's overlap makes it look like two arrows into H, so read arrow ends, not the line's path.

understand.title: The must-check list, explained
understand.text: Node size equals flux: the caption must say so, and the sizes must come from the same normalised flux as the edges. Without it, size is decoration and the picture cannot be compared across conditions.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: Size is a weak channel for numbers: area is judged poorly. Overlapping arrows (here the H2 to OH arrow passes behind the H node) suggest a connection with H that is not in the data. A snapshot at one condition hides how the pathway changes with T or time, and the layout invites reading position as meaning. Edges that are many and thin become a hairball in large mechanisms.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: The Sankey in F9.6 for conserved flow with stages. A matrix of species by reaction (stoichiometry table) for large mechanisms. A ranked table of reaction fluxes for exact numbers. A directed graph with edges bundled for large networks.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add a numeric flux label at each edge, thicken edges on a log scale, and shade the dominant path from fuel to water.

steps.title: Net production rate of a species
steps.note: The reaction fluxes q_r drawn as edges, weighted by the stoichiometry.

steps.title: Flux through a node
steps.note: One common definition for node size: half the total production plus consumption.

worked.title: Is OH a net source or sink here?
worked.problem: Three reactions with fluxes (arbitrary units): H + O2 -> OH + O (q1 = 0.50), O + H2 -> OH + H (q2 = 0.45), OH + H2 -> H2O + H (q3 = 1.00). Find the net production of OH and the node flux F.

solution.text: Net production of OH: it is made by 1 and 2, consumed by 3.

worked.answer: OH is a slight net sink (-0.05) with a large throughput of 0.975: a hub, almost in steady state.

analyze.q: OH is the biggest node but nearly a zero net producer. Why is it still important?
analyze.hint: Think of a hub in steady state.

analyze.q: What information is lost when this graph is a single snapshot?
analyze.hint: What changes with time and temperature?

evaluate.q: Is a graph of 8 species enough to explain a mechanism of 50 species and 300 reactions?
evaluate.hint: What would you filter, and how?

create: Redraw with edges coloured by reaction class and the main path highlighted, avoiding every edge-node overlap.
Make a flux graph at two temperatures and place them side by side.

checks.q: What does the node area encode?
checks.answer: The net flux through the species.

checks.q: A node has fluxes in of 0.6 and 0.2 and out of 0.8. Net production and F?
checks.hint: Sign convention and half the sum.

checks.q: The picture is drawn at one time. What would you plot to see whether the dominant pathway changes in time?
checks.hint: Compare snapshots at progress variable values.
checks.answer: A sequence of graphs or a time-resolved Sankey with the same layout and a fixed scale; compare the dominant path at ignition and in the burnt gas.
